explanation: Availability is defined by when 'the system could actually use it', which is a receipt time. Nearly all research history is backfilled and has no local receipt. Many sources carry only a date: daily bars, fundamentals keyed by filing or period date, earnings dates without before-open or after-close timing, and corporate-action announcement dates. EDGAR's filing date can differ from its acceptance timestamp. One engineer will stamp the publication date at 00:00, or the publication timestamp with zero latency, and so leak. Another will add a latency allowance or roll to the next session. Backtest P&L and promotion decisions then differ. This is the main leakage path the point-in-time store must close, and Chapter 11 makes dataset eligibility depend on it without saying how.
proposed_resolution: Store availability_time together with an availability_basis enum. CAPTURED: live first observation on the canonical production host. PUBLISHED_PLUS_ALLOWANCE: the provider's publication timestamp plus a conservative per-source latency allowance from the source registry. DATE_ONLY_NEXT_SESSION: available at the next regular-session open of the instrument's primary venue after that date ends in the source's timezone. For EDGAR, use acceptanceDateTime, not the filing date. Each strategy artifact declares which bases it accepts. Replay tests shift publication times and assert that features move only at availability_time.
verifier_note: Quotes verified. Grep finds no rule for receipt-less or date-only data anywhere in the book. This also covers which host's capture is canonical (the reason I refuted the separate Mac/AWS ingestion-writer issue).

disposition.resolution: Resolved with an explicit availability_basis rule. Sources without vintages use the capture rule: a value captured by the end of its observation day is available at receipt, a backfill at 23:59:59 of the observation day in the source's zone, flagged availability_estimated_backfill. Bars are available at end plus the source's publication lag. SEC facts are available at acceptance, else at the end of the filed day. Every strategy feature must declare availability_basis from BAR_CLOSE_PLUS_LAG, PUBLISHED_PLUS_ALLOWANCE, DATE_ONLY_NEXT_SESSION or CAPTURED.
disposition.residual: PUBLISHED_PLUS_ALLOWANCE and DATE_ONLY_NEXT_SESSION are declared but no ingested dataset uses them yet (no earnings dates or corporate actions are ingested); the strict parser enforces the enum, but no test submits an unknown basis.

title: The point-in-time store has no knowledge-time or supersedes fields, and no rule for datasets that lack vintages

locations.quote: Corrections create new versions; they do not silently alter a historical experiment.
The feature contract includes entity, event time, availability time, feature version, value, unit, missingness reason and provenance.
Estimate revisions require point-in-time vendor snapshots.
A revised macro series should use its historical vintage.

explanation: The book states the as-of principle: Chapter 3 line 47, Chapter 7 line 29, and Chapter 11 line 35 ('Trailing figures must use reports available at the decision time'). It gives no data model to implement it. The feature contract has no recorded or knowledge time and no supersedes link, so the store cannot answer 'value as known at T' for a corrected or restated key. Line 13 also leaves open whether a correction becomes a new dataset version (system time) or a new row available at the correction's own publication time. The book also never says what to do with a dataset bought today that has only restated values and no vintages, which is common for fundamentals. One engineer will use it, with leakage; another will bar it.
proposed_resolution: Make the normalized and derived layers bitemporal. Each row carries (entity, event_time, availability_time, recorded_time, version, supersedes_id, dataset_version). A correction is a new row whose availability_time is the correction's own publication time. as_of(T) returns, for each key, the latest version with availability_time ≤ T. Experiment manifests pin a content hash or recorded_time ceiling. The registry tags each dataset with pit_grade ∈ {VENDOR_VINTAGE, CAPTURED_FORWARD, RESTATED_ONLY}. RESTATED_ONLY data may appear in labelled research views but is barred from promotion evidence.
verifier_note: Quotes verified. I narrowed the claim and lowered severity from high to medium. The original said the book never states what a backtest should see, which is wrong: it does state the as-of principle in three places. What is missing is the bitemporal fields and the rule for restated-only datasets.

disposition.resolution: ADR-0015: the observation table is bitemporal (available_time plus known_from/known_to and supersedes); a restatement is a later publication, a silent correction closes the previous version's knowledge interval, and as_of(t) never sees a later publication. Datasets declare vintage_support; one without vintages is reconstructed only from what this system captured.
disposition.residual: Barring restated-only data from promotion evidence waits for the promotion gate (I5).

title: The 'untouched' holdout has no access control, reuse limit or consumption rule, so repeated agent candidates overfit it

locations.quote: An untouched holdout must remain untouched after a disappointing result.

Use chronological training, validation and untouched test periods. In walk-forward evaluation, train only on past data, choose parameters on an inner validation period, and evaluate on the next unseen segment.
| R03 | Rigorous quantitative foundations | Research laboratory | Reproducible experiments and untouched evaluation |
Maintain a complete trial register so that repeated candidate generation is visible.

explanation: Agents generate candidates autonomously, and Chapter 20 allows automatic promotion. If every candidate in a family is scored on the same 'untouched' test period and the best is promoted, that period has become a validation set. The trial register makes the repetition visible but does not stop it. Nothing defines who may read holdout results, how many evaluations a holdout allows, whether walk-forward outer segments count as untouched, or what replaces a holdout once used. Two implementations would give very different false-promotion rates.
proposed_resolution: Register holdouts as access-controlled date ranges per hypothesis family (strategy class + universe + label). Only the evaluator service reads holdout data, and research workers and agents never see per-period holdout results. Each holdout evaluation needs a frozen artifact hash, is written to the trial register, and is allowed once per hash. After K family-level evaluations (owner-set, default 1) the holdout is marked CONSUMED, and the next holdout is forward data recorded after that time (shadow or paper). Promotion evidence must cite an unconsumed holdout result.
verifier_note: Quotes verified. Grep for holdout, held-out and untouched finds no access, reuse or consumption rule anywhere in the book.

disposition.resolution: Resolved. The holdout belongs to a pre-registered experiment and is consumed at most once, by the OWNER or the SYSTEM evaluator, never an AGENT. Every attempt, granted or refused, is logged. A dataset view reaching into the holdout needs a grant issued by the registry (a hand-made grant is refused); a non-holdout trial whose manifest reaches the holdout is refused, and leaked returns fail the trial, which still counts.

title: No canonical strategy-spec and evidence schema: four partial field lists, none matching requirement RES-01

locations.quote: Its registry entry includes author, training interval, evaluation manifest, allowed markets, expected horizon, capacity estimate, expiration and rollback predecessor.
The experiment artifact contains hypothesis, manifest, search history, fold results, uncertainty, stress results, rejected alternatives and a signed promotion recommendation.
Each candidate needs an information set, signal equation, position rule, execution rule, cost model, invalidation condition and evidence manifest.
Start every experiment with a hypothesis, universe, information clock, execution rule, cost model, benchmark, parameter-search budget and rejection criterion.

explanation: The repository's requirement RES-01 (docs/requirements/register.md line 123) asks for a registry with hypothesis, equations, variables and units, causal features, rules, costs, capacity, risk limits, failure conditions, splits, baselines, sensitivity, stress and promotion evidence. The book spreads this over four lists that do not agree. The Chapter 20 registry entry, the record the promotion service checks, has no hypothesis, equations, entry/exit/sizing rules, cost model, risk limits, validation or holdout intervals, or baselines. The Chapter 7 artifact has no capacity, allowed markets or expiry. The rules-only ablation that R04 requires (Chapter 1 line 12) appears in none of them. Schemas built from different chapters will disagree on what a promotable artifact must carry.
proposed_resolution: Define two hashed, versioned schemas. StrategySpec holds: hypothesis; equation IDs plus code hash; features (id, version, availability_basis, freshness budget); universe rule; entry, exit and invalidation rules; sizing rule; execution rule (timing, order type, price-bound source, expiry); cost-model version; capacity method and estimate; risk limits; data dependencies with rights references. EvidenceBundle holds: train, validation and holdout intervals; trial-register reference; baselines (cash, buy-and-hold, volatility-capped passive, rules-only ablation); sensitivity grid; stress results; uncertainty records; shadow and paper results. The promotion service rejects any status transition while a required field is missing, and the terminal labels such candidates 'incomplete'.
verifier_note: Quotes verified, and the RES-01 text was found in docs/requirements/register.md. I corrected two overstatements and lowered severity from high to medium. Chapter 7 line 45 does name the list whose absence makes a candidate 'incomplete'. Chapter 20 lines 15 and 17 independently require stress outcomes and robustness to parameter perturbation, so a promotion service following Chapter 20 would not pass a candidate with no stress or sensitivity evidence. What remains is that no single schema exists.

disposition.resolution: Resolved. StrategySpec is one strict, hashed, versioned schema holding every RES-01 field (hypothesis, equations, variables with units, causal features, data requirements, rules, costs, capacity, risk limits, validation plan, baselines, sensitivity and stress plans, required promotion evidence); unknown, missing or out-of-range fields are refused. Promotion evidence is typed by kind (REPLAY_EXACT, CORE_REPLAY_MATCH, WALK_FORWARD_OOS, PAIRED_BOOTSTRAP, HOLDOUT, COST_SENSITIVITY, STRESS, ...) and a transition without the required evidence is refused.
disposition.residual: The evidence bundle is the promotion service's typed evidence records, not a separately versioned schema document.

title: Bar interval convention and cross-market 'rebalance date' alignment are undefined

locations.quote: Record the bar construction version and how incomplete bars are treated. A strategy cannot use the final high or close of a bar before the bar is complete.
At rebalance date $t$, define a past-return score over a documented interval, optionally skipping the most recent period:
Use timezone-aware calendars for display and market rules, UTC for storage, and immutable calendar versions for replay.

explanation: The book never says whether a bar's timestamp is its start or its end, and never gives a bar record its own availability time. Eq. 15.2 and Chapter 15 line 23 ('Rank only instruments eligible at that date') define cross-sectional momentum at a rebalance 'date'. For a US, India and EU universe, a date-keyed join at an Indian or EU decision instant picks up the same date's US close, which is still in the future. Chapter 7 line 7 ('only data whose availability time precedes its decision') would prevent this if bars carried an availability time, but the bar definition never connects to that rule.
proposed_resolution: Store bars as [start_utc, end_utc) with availability_time = end + the venue's official-close publication lag, or the capture time if later. Forbid calendar-date joins in research and live code: every join is 'latest row with availability_time ≤ decision instant (UTC)'. Define each rebalance as a UTC instant per market. FX rates used in a decision must also have availability ≤ the decision instant. Add a fixture with US, NSE and EU instruments on one date asserting that no US close is visible at an earlier-closing market's decision instant.
verifier_note: Quotes verified. Grep finds no bar start/end convention. Severity lowered from high to medium: Chapter 7 line 7's availability rule already forbids the leak if applied to bars. The gap is the bar record fields and the per-market meaning of 'date' in Eq. 15.2.

disposition.resolution: Resolved. Bars are stored as [start, end) with an availability time (end plus the source's publication lag), and corrections are later versions. Every read is 'latest version with availability time <= decision instant' at a UTC decision instant, never a calendar-date join; the research bar series and the point-in-time store agree at every availability boundary. IBKR historical bars follow the same rule.
disposition.residual: Cross-market rebalancing is not exercised: the engine refuses instruments whose currency or settlement cycle differs from the run's (USD, T+1).

title: Promotion-gate parameters have no home or unset behaviour, and the gate utility does not say whether it is net of trading costs or all-in

locations.quote: One example gate requires the lower bound of a paired block-bootstrap improvement interval to exceed a positive economic hurdle, with sufficient effective sample size and acceptable stress outcomes. The confidence level, block method, hurdle and trial correction must be fixed before evaluation.
The project promotion protocol uses these principles without claiming a universal sample-count threshold.
Model research/cloud costs separately and then report an all-in economic result as well.
The sample Sharpe statistic is $\bar r/s_r$ per observation.

explanation: Chapter 20 requires the gate parameters to be fixed in advance but gives them no home: they are not in the policy contents, the registry entry or the deployment record. It also does not say that automatic promotion is disabled while they are unset. The fail-closed principles in Chapter 1 line 43 and Chapter 6 line 49 cover only the deployment record and capital caps. 'Sufficient' n_eff and 'acceptable' stress have no field. The paired utility is 'net return' (Chapter 20 line 13), net of fees per Chapter 4 line 50, but Chapter 7 says a broker-positive strategy can lose money all-in, and nothing says which of the two the gate uses. Drawdown penalties are path-dependent, and the book does not say whether utility is computed per block or per resampled path. Sharpe is defined on raw per-observation returns, with 'show the convention' as the only rule.
proposed_resolution: Make the promotion protocol an owner-signed policy object with required fields: confidence level, block-length rule, hurdle in bps per period net of trading costs, minimum n_eff and its estimator, minimum calendar span and regime coverage, trial-correction method, utility coefficients, stress thresholds, and an all-in gate (expected contribution after strategy-attributable data, model and compute costs must be > 0). If any field is unset, automatic promotion is disabled and promotion is owner-only. Compute utility on each resampled full path. Compute Sharpe on returns in excess of the cash alternative, with K taken from the instrument's calendar. With no incumbent, compare against cash and the passive baseline (Chapter 7 line 35).
verifier_note: Quotes verified. Narrowed and lowered from high to medium. The book deliberately leaves threshold values to the owner ('example protocol'), and it already names cash and passive exposure as baselines (Chapter 7 line 35), which answers the original's 'no incumbent' question. The real gaps are where the parameters live, fail-closed behaviour when they are unset, and trading-net versus all-in.

disposition.resolution: Resolved. The promotion protocol is an owner-approved object with exactly these fields: confidence, replications, mean block, statistic, utility coefficients, hurdle per period (net of trading costs), min n_eff, min OOS observations, min OOS Sharpe, max PBO, min DSR, required cost multiplier, max stress drawdown, holdout minimum difference, min paper days and seed. A missing or extra field refuses the protocol, so no gate can run unset; gate verdicts are recomputed under it, and evidence fails if the protocol was approved after the evaluation started.
disposition.residual: There is no all-in (operating-cost) gate: all-in costs default to 0 and are labelled NOT CONFIGURED.

title: Corporate-action handling in research is undefined: 'causally adjusted', 'corporate-action version', delisting exits, and actions between decision and transmission

locations.quote: Use total-return prices when the research question includes distributions. Use unadjusted execution prices for order and ledger reconstruction.
Let $r_t=\log(P_t/P_{t-1})$ on causally adjusted observations.
validate source freshness and corporate-action version
Include delisted instruments and actual filing availability.

explanation: The book never defines 'causally adjusted' or 'corporate-action version'. Vendor back-adjusted series apply factors from later actions. Return ratios survive that, but price levels do not, so minimum-price universe filters, breakout levels compared with live quotes, and lot-affordability checks all leak. Delisted names must be included, but nothing says how a held position exits: delisting proceeds, last trade, or dropped. Dropping it reintroduces survivorship bias. Total-return series do not say whether dividends are gross or net of the owner's withholding. A split taking effect between decision (after the close) and next-session transmission leaves the intent's quantity and limit in pre-split units, because A15 checks the corporate-action version only at decision time.
proposed_resolution: Store raw prices plus point-in-time corporate-action events (announcement availability_time, ex-date, factor or cash amount, successor instrument). Compute features by adjusting only within the lookback window, using actions with ex-date ≤ decision time; never read stored back-adjusted levels. Total-return series apply the withholding rate implied by the deployment record's owner residency. For delistings, use actual proceeds or successor terms from the corporate-action feed; if unknown, apply a conservative haircut recorded in the manifest. Each intent carries its corporate-action version, and pretrade rejects it if any action's ex-date falls between decision and transmission.
verifier_note: Quotes verified. Severity lowered from high to medium. I checked numerically that a uniform future back-adjustment factor leaves the TREND_DAILY_V1 score (difference of log-price EMAs) and log-return volatility unchanged (max difference 1e-15), so the first strategy's signal is unaffected. Leakage is confined to level-based features and filters, delisting exits and the split window. For buys, the Chapter 13 price collar would partly catch a pre-split limit.

disposition.resolution: Not implemented: no corporate-action feed or adjustment exists in research (the core side is BR-LED-16). The research engine documents corporate actions as not handled and runs on SYNTHETIC fixtures without them.
disposition.owner: I4 (corporate-action data, DAT-03) with I5 (feature adjustment, delisting exits)
disposition.missing: Point-in-time corporate-action events, in-window causal adjustment, delisting proceeds, and a pretrade check for an ex-date between decision and transmission.

title: The research-proposal contract has no typed evidence, instrument identity or timestamps, so the validation Chapter 19 requires cannot be performed

locations.quote: "required": ["schema_version", "job_id", "hypothesis", "evidence", "horizon_seconds", "assumptions", "abstain", "reason"]
"evidence": {"type": "array", "maxItems": 50, "items": {"type": "string", "maxLength": 500}}
Validate cited evidence, numeric ranges, instrument identity, timestamps and policy scope separately.
A useful forecast output includes horizon, distribution or quantiles, confidence-calibration version, evidence references, assumptions, invalidation conditions and an abstention reason.

An uncertainty record includes target definition, horizon, observation count, effective-sample diagnostic, training interval, evaluation interval, calibration method, confidence interval method and data version. Model output that lacks these fields cannot be treated as quantified trading confidence.

explanation: The only machine contract for agent output has free-text evidence strings, no instrument identifier, no timestamps, no dataset version and no invalidation conditions. Chapter 19 line 13 requires checking cited evidence, instrument identity and timestamps, and Chapter 11 line 29 requires checking numerical claims against source spans. Neither can be done against this schema. 'additionalProperties': false means adding these fields requires a new schema version. No forecast contract carrying the Chapter 19 line 15 fields exists. The schema also does not tie abstain=true to the other fields: horizon_seconds and hypothesis remain required on an abstention.
proposed_resolution: Publish schema_version 2. Evidence becomes typed references {source_id, dataset_version, locator/span, content_hash}. Add instrument_ids and an observation-time window. Add an optional forecast block; if present, it requires every Chapter 4 uncertainty-record field plus invalidation_conditions. Add if/then rules: abstain=true forbids a forecast block and relaxes hypothesis and horizon; abstain=false requires a hypothesis and at least one evidence reference. A proposal without a forecast block is labelled QUALITATIVE and cannot feed a strategy feature.
verifier_note: Quotes verified. Reclassified from contradiction to omission. Chapter 4 line 54 is consistent with the schema (a proposal without these fields simply is not quantified confidence), and Chapter 19 line 15 says 'useful', not 'required'. The model ID and input artifact hashes can be recovered through job_id from the job record (Chapter 19 line 9), so I dropped that part. What holds is the Chapter 19 line 13 validation gap.

disposition.resolution: The core accepts research_proposal schema version 2 beside v1. Version 2 carries typed evidence references (dataset, observation or document-span id, content hash, observed and available times), instrument and research-entity ids (instrument ids are checked against the instrument master), the job's as-of instant, an observation-time window, an optional forecast block (target, horizon, unit, interval or quantiles, calibration, the Chapter 4 uncertainty record, invalidation conditions) and abstain-dependent rules. The core validates v2 strictly: no evidence or window after as_of, references inside the window, and checks of syntax, counts and forecast ordering. It records the proposal with a core-assigned label (ABSTENTION, QUALITATIVE, FORECAST_UNCALIBRATED, FORECAST_QUANTIFIED) and still changes only the proposals table. The agent layer emits v2 with every typed field taken from the job or from the store provenance of the spans that verified claims cite, never from model output; a claim is evidence only when every span it cites yields a typed reference.
disposition.residual: Version 1 (free-text evidence) is still accepted. Agent answers never carry a forecast block, because no calibration record exists, so no agent proposal is FORECAST_QUANTIFIED. No proposal feeds a strategy feature or an order.

title: Eq. 4.2 n_eff is undefined or unbounded for negative autocorrelation sums, and its estimator is unspecified where it feeds the promotion gate

locations.quote: n_{\mathrm{eff}}\approx\frac{n}{1+2\sum_{k=1}^{K}\rho_k}
This approximation needs a sensible truncation and stationarity assumptions.
with sufficient effective sample size and acceptable stress outcomes

explanation: When the estimated Σρ̂_k ≤ −0.5, the denominator is zero or negative, so n_eff is infinite or negative. As the sum approaches −0.5 from above, n_eff grows without bound. With ρ̂1 = −0.3 and K = 1, n_eff = 2.5n. That value is mathematically right for a truly anti-correlated series, but estimated from noisy sample autocorrelations of bid-ask-bounce or mean-reverting P&L, it overstates the evidence. Neither the truncation K nor the ρ estimator is specified, and the Chapter 20 gate consumes 'sufficient effective sample size' without naming either.
proposed_resolution: For gate use: n_eff = min(n, n_nonoverlap, n / max(1, 1 + 2·Σ_{k=1}^{K} ρ̂_k)), with K from Geyer's initial-positive-sequence rule, or K = label horizon in bars. n_nonoverlap = n / label_horizon. Report it next to the block-bootstrap interval, and gate on the more conservative of the two.
verifier_note: Formula and arithmetic verified (1/(1−0.6) = 2.5). Severity lowered from medium to low, and the explanation corrected: n_eff > n is not by itself an error, since the formula is the standard variance-of-the-mean correction. The book also labels it a diagnostic needing 'sensible truncation'. What holds is the undefined region and the unspecified estimator for gate use.

disposition.resolution: Resolved. n_eff follows eq. 4.2 with a declared truncation K and returns None where 1 + 2 sum rho <= 0; the gate form is bounded: min(n, n / label_horizon, n / max(1, 1 + 2 sum rho_k)). The study's N_EFF gate is computed on the paired out-of-sample differences and reported next to the bootstrap interval.

title: Purge and embargo lengths and placement are not specified

locations.quote: Purge overlapping label windows at boundaries; add an embargo when adjacent examples share future outcomes.
**Embargo:** excluded interval reducing overlap in evaluation information.

explanation: The book does not say how long the embargo is or on which side of the test segment it sits, and does not say whether execution delay extends the purge. In walk-forward, the last training labels (t_end + h_label) reach into the test period unless purged by at least h_label + execution delay. For a 20-day label on daily bars, that is up to 20 days of leakage. Engineers will pick different gaps, and promotion evidence will differ with them.
proposed_resolution: Purge every training sample whose interval [t, t + h_label + execution_delay] intersects the evaluation segment's label span [start, end + h_label]. In walk-forward, require a gap between train end and test start of at least h_label + execution_delay. In any split where training data follows a test segment, add a post-test embargo of max(h_label, lookback of the longest autocorrelated feature). Record both lengths in the manifest, and have the evaluator reject manifests below these minimums.
verifier_note: Quotes verified. Grep finds no purge or embargo length anywhere in the book. Chapter 7 does say which samples to purge (overlapping label windows), so the gap is lengths, placement and execution delay.

disposition.resolution: Resolved. The spec refuses purge_sessions below label_horizon_sessions + execution_delay_sessions; the purge and embargo are part of the hashed spec and manifest, and the evaluator (walk-forward, purged k-fold, CPCV) purges training whose label interval meets a test run's label span on either side of the run, and embargoes training that follows a test run.

title: Trend weight mapping has no aggregate cap or session-level denominator, and 'unallocated cash' collides with the ledger bucket name

locations.quote: A long-only mapping uses $w_t=\min(w_{max},k\max(0,z_t))$, with a no-trade band around current weight to reduce turnover.
Weights use a consistent denominator: account equity or authorized trading capital, explicitly identified.
uses price-bounded orders and leaves unallocated cash idle
Separately track policy buckets: unallocated capital, session allocations, protected proceeds, order reservations and operational buffers.

explanation: Weights are computed per instrument. Over TREND_DAILY_V1's multi-name universe, Σw can reach N·w_max > 1 in a cash-only account. Pretrade then rejects whichever orders arrive last, so holdings depend on submission order. Chapter 6 offers only account equity or authorized capital as the denominator. For a strategy inside a session, it does not say whether that means session seed, session marked equity (at which mark) or the account, and each gives different exposure as the session approaches its target. Chapter 15 also uses 'unallocated cash' for idle cash inside a session, while Chapters 9 and 10 use 'unallocated' for the account bucket that funds successors.
proposed_resolution: Weights are fractions of session marked equity, valued at the executable bid, minus the operational buffer. After computing raw w_i, apply per-name caps, then scale proportionally so that Σw_i ≤ 1 − cash_reserve, before diffing against current-plus-pending holdings. Rename the Chapter 15 term to 'session idle cash', and reserve `unallocated` in domain types for the account-level bucket.
verifier_note: Quotes verified. Chapter 15 line 25's projection onto the feasible set applies to the cross-sectional inverse-volatility weights, not to the time-series mapping, so the aggregate-cap gap holds for TREND_DAILY_V1. The terminology collision is real but minor; ADR-0008 already uses `unallocated` only for the account bucket.

disposition.resolution: Resolved in one sizing implementation, research.sizing.plan_orders, which the backtest engine and the strategy runner both call: target weights are fractions of marked equity, capped per name, then scaled to min(aggregate_cap, 1 - cash_reserve) over every target before the diff against current holdings (owned plus pending buys minus pending sells; BR-DAT-02); the spec refuses sizing above the risk limits. The terminology collision stays avoided (`unallocated` is only the account-level owner).
disposition.residual: Exposure at runtime is the session's, not the artifact's: every principal's orders in the session count as the artifact's current holdings, so one artifact per session is the documented rule (BR-DAT-02).

title: Licence-driven raw-data deletion conflicts with 'replay must reproduce', and artifact status after deletion is unspecified

locations.quote: Deleting expired raw data may affect reproducibility; preserve allowed hashes, manifests and derived evidence where the license permits.
Replaying the same manifest must reproduce the same economic events.
Statuses are proposed, reproducible, validated, paper, eligible, active, quarantined and retired.

explanation: Chapter 7 makes manifest replay an absolute requirement, and `reproducible` is a promotion status. Chapter 11 accepts that licence-driven deletion can break replay. The book does not say whether an active or eligible artifact whose evidence can no longer be replayed keeps its status, can be renewed, or loses `reproducible`.
proposed_resolution: The source registry records retention_end per dataset. Promotion sets artifact expiration ≤ min(retention_end) over its evidence datasets, unless the required derived features are licensed for retention and stored with hashes. When evidence data is deleted, flag the artifact EVIDENCE_EXPIRED. It may run until its existing expiration but cannot be renewed or re-promoted without new evidence.
verifier_note: Quotes verified. Severity lowered from medium to low: this is a governance gap with no immediate effect on money, and Chapter 20's registry 'expiration' field already gives the needed hook.

disposition.resolution: Partly resolved: the mechanism exists and is tested, but nothing feeds it real data. Raw payloads carry a retention deadline and deletion time (ADR-0015 raw layer). A research manifest's dataset entry may state retention_until. Registration refuses an expiry after the evaluation data's retention, and every expiry check (activation, automatic selection, automatic shadow promotion, the strategy runner) uses min(expires_on, retention_until of every evidence dataset). record_evidence_deletion (OWNER or SYSTEM, append-only, once per dataset) marks every artifact resting on that dataset EVIDENCE_EXPIRED: it may run until its expiry, every upward transition is refused, and there is no renewal.
disposition.owner: I4 (retention metadata and deletion process) and I5 (manifests)
disposition.missing: Wiring to data. Research manifests (research/manifest.py) never write retention_until, although the data registry has retention_days and the raw layer has retention_until_ns (no source sets it yet). No data-retention process calls record_evidence_deletion. Until both exist, no real artifact's expiry is bounded by retention, and none becomes EVIDENCE_EXPIRED.

title: Source-registry 'allowed uses' and 'model-processing permission' are unenumerated, single-valued per source, and have no per-provider or per-host scope

locations.quote: Each entry records provider, dataset, transport, entitlement, allowed uses, redistribution restrictions, retention, model-processing permission, update frequency, availability clock, quality checks and estimated cost.
Record provider lineage to understand correlated failures.
"model_processing_rights_verified": false,

explanation: 'Allowed uses' and 'availability clock' are not enumerated. An automated-trading platform needs distinct rights for display, non-display (algorithmic) use, derived data, submission to each cloud-model provider (the owner plans OpenAI, xAI and others), and storage or processing location (Mac vs AWS region). The per-source 'model-processing permission' is a single value, so it cannot say 'provider A yes, provider B no'. Line 23 requires recording provider lineage, but lineage is not a registry field. The deployment record adds one global boolean that, read as a gate, would clear every source for every provider.
proposed_resolution: Registry fields: rights {display, non_display_trading, derived_data, redistribution, model_providers_allowed[], hosts_or_regions_allowed[]}; licence_start and licence_end; retention_end; upstream_lineage[]; timestamp_semantics and timezone; availability_latency_allowance; pit_grade; rate_limit_policy; cost. Gate each action per (source, use, host, model provider). Make the deployment boolean a derived value (AND over enabled sources) or remove it.
verifier_note: Quotes verified. The registry does carry a per-source model-processing permission, so the global boolean is not the only control as written. The confirmed gap is the missing per-provider and per-host scope, the unenumerated uses, and lineage present in the prose but absent from the field list.

disposition.resolution: ADR-0015 enumerates allowed uses (display, non_display, storage, derived_storage, redistribution, model_processing_cloud, model_processing_local). Model-provider scope is decided per request by the data-use gate: the dataset must grant cloud processing, and the provider's retention, training use, residency and tier must satisfy the owner policy; unknown facts block. The deployment record's global boolean is unused.
disposition.residual: Upstream lineage and licence start/end are not registry fields yet.

title: Feature contract lacks the validity window, warm-up state and freshness-budget owner that Chapters 5 and 26 check against; restart behaviour is unspecified

locations.quote: The feature contract includes entity, event time, availability time, feature version, value, unit, missingness reason and provenance.
Record warm-up status explicitly. The strategy must reject an input vector whose feature version or validity window differs from the approved model contract.
Resume only after warm-up and feature-state consistency checks.

explanation: Chapter 5 requires rejecting inputs by validity window and recording warm-up status, but the Chapter 11 feature contract has neither field, and 'validity window' is never defined. Chapter 11 line 25 says freshness budgets 'depend on strategy horizon' without saying where they are declared. Missingness reasons appear only as examples. On restart, one engineer persists EWMA state and another re-warms from live data. Re-warming a slow daily EMA from live data would keep the strategy disabled for months.
proposed_resolution: Add valid_from/valid_until, warm_up_state {COLD, WARMING, WARM} with min_observations, and an enumerated missingness_reason {NOT_REPORTED, PROVIDER_DELAY, SOURCE_GAP, NOT_APPLICABLE, QUARANTINED}. Declare freshness budgets per feature in the StrategySpec, and check them at decision and at transmission. On restart, rebuild feature state by deterministic replay from the point-in-time store over at least the warm-up length, then compare with the persisted snapshot. A mismatch blocks entries.
verifier_note: Quotes verified. Chapter 5 line 3 lists 'warm-up condition' as part of each feature's definition, but the per-row contract the strategy checks lacks warm-up state and validity window, so the mismatch is real.

disposition.resolution: research.features builds one row per instrument and declared feature at each decision. A row holds a value or exactly one enumerated missing reason (NOT_REPORTED, PROVIDER_DELAY, SOURCE_GAP, NOT_APPLICABLE, QUARANTINED), the warm-up state (COLD, WARMING, WARM) and a validity window that starts at the availability of the newest input and lasts min(validity_window_s, freshness_budget_s). Spec schema v2 declares validity_window_s and the freshness budget per feature, and a spec whose feature ids or versions differ from the implementation is refused when the strategy is built. The runner blocks an instrument whose rows are unusable at the decision (FEATURE_INVALID, FEATURE_OUTSIDE_VALIDITY_WINDOW) and never transmits an intent whose features have expired (FEATURE_EXPIRED). No feature state is persisted: every decision rebuilds the strategy from the point-in-time store. At a process's first cycle the runner re-warms as of its journal's latest decision and compares rows and targets; a MISMATCH blocks new buys, including buys planned before the restart.
disposition.residual: The restart check compares the journal's latest decision only, and a mismatch blocks entries for the process's lifetime rather than until an owner acknowledges it. The backtest builds no feature rows, so on gappy real data it decides where the runner blocks. Freshness is checked by the runner (at the decision and at transmission), not by the core.

title: TREND_DAILY_V1, the book's own worked candidate, omits the execution rule that Chapter 15 says every candidate needs

locations.quote: It rebalances no more than once per eligible session, uses price-bounded orders and leaves unallocated cash idle.
Each candidate needs an information set, signal equation, position rule, execution rule, cost model, invalidation condition and evidence manifest.
Execute after the observation becomes available.
A strategy approved for continuous matching must not automatically participate in an auction.

explanation: The first strategy, the one the I5 critical path builds, decides on a completed daily bar but never says when it submits, which reference price sets the limit (prior close or a fresh quote at transmission), how long the intent lives, whether it may join the opening auction, or what happens to an unfilled remainder (carried over or regenerated next day). This breaks the book's own Chapter 15 line 3 requirement. A bound fixed at the prior close fills buys mostly on gap-downs. Backtest and paper diverge unless both use one rule, and a carried-over intent plus a new daily intent duplicates exposure.
proposed_resolution: Specify the rule as follows. Decide after the official close becomes available. Submit in the next regular session, between open + N minutes and close − M minutes, with no auctions. At transmission, set the limit to min(model bound, collar around a fresh validated quote). Use TIF DAY, expiring at the end of that window. Cancel any unfilled remainder and never carry it over; the next decision recomputes from current-plus-pending holdings. The backtest applies the identical rule to next-session data.
verifier_note: Quotes verified. ADR-0009 already fixes limit-only, TIF DAY and regular-hours-only for initial eligibility. What remains open is the submission window, the price-bound reference and the carry-over rule.

disposition.resolution: Spec schema v2 declares rules.execution.submission_window: open + N to close - M minutes, no auctions, the limit referenced at transmission, the remainder cancelled at the window's end. research.execution applies it identically for the backtest and the strategy runner. The window comes from the calendar's session hours (early closes included). At transmission the limit is min(model bound, mid x (1 + collar)) for a buy (the max for a sell), from a quote validated by the core's own rules. The order carries the window's end as its deadline, and its remainder is cancelled at the window's end with a deterministic cancel id, also in a cycle that refuses or fails to decide. Nothing is carried over: the next decision recomputes from current plus pending holdings. Same-bar fills stay refused.
disposition.residual: The core does not enforce the window after transmission: the runner's cancel ends it, so a runner that is down at the window's end leaves the remainder working until the close. The backtest references the session open (daily bars carry no quote), assumes uniform intraday volume and still fills on the whole day's bar: optimistic, labelled and not modelled (docs/strategy/README.md).

title: The cost model has no schema: side- and jurisdiction-specific charges and the units of the impact model are unspecified

locations.quote: Net P&L includes commissions, venue fees, spread, slippage, market impact, borrow where permitted, financing, currency conversion and applicable transaction taxes.
A simple impact sensitivity model is $I=Y\sigma\sqrt{Q/V}$, where $Q$ is trade size and $V$ relevant market volume.
$c$ a conservative per-share cost allowance

explanation: The book lists cost categories but gives no functional form. Real charges are asymmetric by side and jurisdiction: US regulatory fees on sells only, Indian STT, stamp duty, exchange charges and GST, and EU financial-transaction taxes on some purchases. Many charges are proportional to notional rather than per share, or have minimums, which the per-share c in Eq. 6.4 cannot express. The impact formula gives no units for σ and V: annualized versus daily σ alone changes the cost by about √252 ≈ 15.9x. The backtest, the Eq. 6.4 sizer and the Chapter 9 reservation fee envelope could each use a different model.
proposed_resolution: Define a versioned CostModel keyed by (jurisdiction, venue, broker, account tier, effective_from). It is a function of (side, qty, price, notional, order_count) that returns itemized charges. Measure σ and V over the same interval as the parent order's horizon, and record Y with its calibration source. Use one implementation for the backtest, sizing, the reservation fee envelope and expected-fee reconciliation.
verifier_note: Quotes verified. √252 = 15.87 recomputed. ADR-0007 names a 'fee model reference' in the policy but defines no schema.

disposition.resolution: Resolved for the research scope. The cost model is a versioned, typed object: fee schedule id (fee.ibkr.us.fixed@2026-10-22, fee.ibkr.us.tiered@2026-10-22), spread and slippage in bps, square-root impact with at least two Y values in stated units, and a sell-side third-party fee flagged UNVERIFIED; fees are exact at ledger scale and side-specific. An instrument without a recorded schedule is refused, and the core replay recomputes every engine commission with the core's own fee model.
disposition.residual: US IBKR Pro schedules only (other jurisdictions are refused, not modelled); the core reservation envelope uses risk/fees.py, a separate implementation that the core replay cross-checks.

title: The order_intent schema cannot link orders to their strategy artifact, decision evidence, currency, TIF or policy as Chapter 30 requires, and there is no table for no-trade decision events

locations.quote: CREATE TABLE order_intent (
An order adds instrument, side, scaled quantity/limit, currency, time-in-force, session, strategy artifact and decision evidence.
Record a decision event even when the result is no trade so that missed opportunities and restraint can be audited.

explanation: order_intent (lines 21-29) has command_id, payload_hash, session_id, instrument_id, side, quantity_units, limit_price_units, deadline_utc_ns and state. It has no currency, time_in_force, strategy artifact, decision evidence or policy hash, all of which Chapter 30 line 7 lists for a command or order. There is no decision-event table, so the no-trade decisions that Chapter 15 requires have no store. Rollback attribution (Chapter 20 line 33), live-versus-backtest comparison and drift-based quarantine all need every order and every no-trade decision tied to the exact artifact and feature snapshot.
proposed_resolution: Add strategy_artifact_hash, decision_event_id, policy_hash, currency and time_in_force to order_intent as first-class columns. Add an append-only decision_event table keyed by the deterministic decision ID: artifact_hash, session_id, instrument_id, decision_bar_id, feature_snapshot_hash, score, desired, current and pending exposure, and outcome {INTENT, NO_TRADE(reason)}.
verifier_note: Quote and schema columns verified. The outbox.payload_json column could carry some of these fields opaquely, but they are not first-class or queryable for attribution, and no decision-event store exists. The schema is labelled 'Proposed', but it still contradicts Chapter 30.

disposition.resolution: Resolved. Orders record currency, time_in_force, policy_hash and strategy_id; for a STRATEGY principal the strategy id is its artifact id `<class>@<16 hex of the artifact hash>`, enforced to equal the authenticated principal. record_strategy_decision stores every evaluated decision (NO_TRADE, INTENT_SUBMITTED, BLOCKED, SKIPPED_STALE_DATA; live or shadow) with the inputs digest, observation time and the ids of the orders it submitted, in the hash-chained event log, with no economic effect. Rejected intents keep their full pretrade decision.
disposition.residual: The link runs from the decision event to the order ids; an order carries only a free-form decision_ref (the strategy runner's names its decision), not a verified decision event id.

title: Mac/AWS single-writer fencing has no authoritative ownership record, epoch or transfer protocol, and the book leaves automatic fenced replacement and manual transfer both open

locations.quote: If a broker cannot enforce fencing, route all account commands through a single credential-owning gateway and require explicit failover reconciliation.
A Mac developer instance and an AWS instance must not simultaneously issue orders under the same ownership assumption.
On cloud-instance termination, preserve durable state and require leader fencing before replacement.
Prefer a single credential-owning gateway with fencing or require manual transfer of execution ownership after reconciliation.
| Split brain | One fenced writer | Rejected stale leader |
Develop on the Mac Studio with isolated environments, pinned dependencies and paper-only credentials.
CREATE TABLE outbox (

explanation: The book requires one fenced execution leader per account (Ch 8 l.37, Ch 28 l.30) but never says what issues or checks the fence. It defines no ownership record, no epoch and no transfer procedure. IBKR has no broker-enforced fencing token, so any fence must be local. SQLite cannot be shared between hosts (Ch 8 l.9, Ch 24 l.19), so a Mac deployment and an AWS deployment each have their own ledger, and each could consider itself 'the single credential-owning gateway'. Ch 24 l.25 ('require leader fencing before replacement') reads as automatic replacement. Ch 24 l.27 offers manual transfer only as an 'or'. Ch 8 l.39 defers only multi-region failover, so single-region automatic failover is neither allowed nor forbidden. Neither order_intent, outbox nor OrderIntent carries an epoch or deployment id, so reconciliation cannot attribute orders sent by a stale host. A Mac paper instance and an AWS paper instance on the same paper account have the same problem.
proposed_resolution: 1) The foundation and first live release have no automatic failover. 2) Each broker account (paper and live separately) has one durable execution_ownership record {account_key, deployment_id, epoch (monotonic), credential_fingerprint, granted_at, granted_by}. 3) Every order_intent and outbox row, and the broker orderRef, carry deployment_id:epoch:command_id, so reconciliation can attribute any order a stale host sent. 4) Transfer is an owner-authorized command: latch the stop on the old host if it is reachable, cancel entries, reconcile, then epoch+1 and green preflight on the new host. If the old host is unreachable or terminated, rotate the broker API credential before granting the new epoch, so the old host physically cannot authenticate. 5) The gateway refuses to start if its credential fingerprint or epoch differs from the record. The outbox refuses to transmit a row with a stale epoch. 6) Live credentials exist only on the deployment the deployment record names. 7) Mac paper and AWS paper use distinct paper accounts, or the same ownership protocol. Tests: a second gateway on the same account refuses to start; a stale-epoch send is rejected; an old-epoch order found at the broker is ingested and attributed as foreign.
verifier_note: All quotes verified. Two sub-claims were overstated and are removed. Ch 24 l.19 says SQLite is not a shared network-filesystem database; it does not say each host keeps its own ledger. Ch 24's paper-only Mac does not contradict Ch 8, because paper orders are still orders. Kind changed from contradiction to ambiguity. Branch ADR-0011 (docs/adr/0011-execution-ownership-and-split-brain.md) already adopts manual transfer, an execution_ownership record with epoch, deployment:epoch order tagging and one credential per account. Three gaps remain open in both the book and the ADR: (a) there is no transfer path when the old host is unreachable or terminated, because ADR-0011 step 2.1 requires the releasing side to emit a signed certificate, so the Ch 24 l.25 termination case can only be fenced by rotating the credential; (b) contracts/ledger_schema.sql and OrderIntent have no epoch or deployment columns; (c) the book text still allows automatic fenced replacement.

disposition.resolution: ADR-0011: one execution_ownership record per account (deployment, monotonic epoch, status, grantor, provenance), acquired only by owner command. A paper or live hand-over needs the previous holder's release certificate (stop latched, no open orders, clean reconciliation) or an explicit owner attestation. Every order carries deployment:epoch:client-id, transmission requires HELD ownership, foreign-tagged or untagged activity latches the stop, and there is no automatic failover.
disposition.residual: Credential rotation for an unreachable or terminated old host is not covered.

title: A restore from backup silently rolls back the stop latch, command-ID dedup, outbox and successor state, enabling duplicate orders and unlatched trading

locations.quote: A restored ledger must reconcile with broker activity that occurred after the backup before it can resume trading.
Stop persists through restart. Start requires owner authority and fresh preflight/reconciliation.
Reusing an identifier with a different payload is an error, not a retry.
Define which events are security critical and retain them according to actual legal and operational requirements.

explanation: A restore returns the ledger to backup time, and everything recorded after the backup is lost. A stop latch set after the backup is gone, so the restored ledger is unlatched, which breaks the invariant that the stop persists. Command IDs and payload hashes recorded after the backup are gone, so a resent command with such an ID is accepted as new and can send a duplicate order. Outbox rows for orders sent after the backup are gone, so reconciliation finds those broker orders and files them in the external-owner bucket (Ch 9 l.49) instead of under their sessions. Reservations and successor allocations recorded after the backup are lost too. The book requires only reconciliation with post-backup broker activity. It does not say the restored state boots latched, how lost orders are re-attributed, or how command-ID reuse is prevented. It also sets no RPO value or economic-journal retention period: Ch 24 l.21 leaves RPO and RTO for the owner to define.
proposed_resolution: 1) A restore always boots STOP_LATCHED with reason RESTORED, whatever the backup's latch state. Only an owner green after review clears it. 2) Ship the append-only economic journal and the command table off-host on every commit, to object storage with object lock. Snapshots then only speed up recovery, and the RPO for economic events and command IDs is effectively zero. Retain the economic journal for at least 7 years after the relevant tax year. 3) Every broker order carries the local command_id in orderRef. After a restore, broker orders and executions are re-attributed to their command and session through that tag. Executions are re-ingested with executions_since from the backup watermark with overlap. If the gap exceeds the API lookback, ingest broker statements and open an exception. 4) Add a ledger incarnation_id to the command-ID namespace and increment it on restore. Tombstone any command ID found at the broker but missing locally, so it cannot be reused. 5) Recompute successor requests from their deterministic keys. Restore drill: back up; submit an order and set the stop; restore; assert the latch is set, the order is attributed, a resend creates no duplicate and there is exactly one successor.
verifier_note: Quotes verified. Branch ADR-0003 item 6 only restates Ch 24 l.21. Under ADR-0010 the recovery gate does not auto-clear by default (auto_resume_after_clean_reconciliation=false), which limits automatic resumption. The latch history, command-ID dedup and outbox attribution are still lost on restore. The retention figure in the resolution is a policy choice, not a legal finding.

disposition.resolution: Restore detection (c41a505): a backup is marked inside the copy, and a database whose writer epoch is not above the <db>.epoch marker, or a non-empty one without it, is a restore. The process start then latches the stop (RESTORED_FROM_BACKUP), opens a blocking exception, turns in-flight and RESERVED orders into UNKNOWN with NEEDS_LOOKUP (never resent) and requires reconciliation before anything else.
disposition.residual: Orders created after the backup are unknown to the restored ledger, so reconciliation treats them as foreign activity (latch) instead of re-attributing them to sessions; there is no continuous off-host journal shipping (RPO undefined).

title: Owner identity and step-up authentication are never defined; R13 'signed policy' contradicts the unsigned schema, and agents on the Mac can act as the owner

locations.quote: Authenticate operator actions, protect sessions, require appropriate reauthentication for sensitive policy changes and use anti-CSRF controls for cookie-based web commands.
| R13 | Human controls settings and code | Signed policy registry | Unauthorized mutation tests |
authorized_by TEXT NOT NULL, effective_at TEXT NOT NULL
if p.get("owner") is not True or p.get("reconciled") is not True:
Authentication supplies identity; it is not accepted from a caller-controlled string.
Claude Code's project-memory mechanism can carry instructions, but it is contextual guidance rather than a security boundary.
Use a local HTTPS control API and server-pushed state updates.

explanation: Every authority rule in the book depends on an owner identity the book never specifies: green and latch clearing, widening limits, budget changes and out-of-envelope promotion. It names no authenticator and no signing-key custody. It gives no freshness window for 'appropriate reauthentication' and no list of sensitive commands. R13 names a 'Signed policy registry', but the proposed policy_version table stores authorized_by as a free string with no signature. On the Mac, Claude Code, research workers and generated code run as the owner's OS user. They can reach the localhost HTTPS control API and any cookie or token stored for it, and Ch 27 l.3 itself says CLAUDE.md is not a boundary. Of the web threats, only CSRF is mentioned; DNS rebinding and same-user local callers are not.
proposed_resolution: Owner authority is a WebAuthn/passkey assertion with user verification (Touch ID or hardware key). Its challenge is the canonical payload hash of the specific command. The server verifies it, and it is valid for that one command only, for at most 60 s. Sensitive commands are listed: green/clear latch, policy create or widen, budget change, deployment-record change, execution-ownership transfer, out-of-envelope promotion, live-mode enable and credential rotation. Add signature, signer_key_id and signed_payload_hash to policy_version and to the deployment record. Services verify them against pinned owner public keys at load and at every activation. The control API validates Host and Origin and binds to loopback or a unix socket, or uses mTLS. No bearer token grants owner authority. Negative test: a same-OS-user process holding the session cookie cannot green or widen a policy without a fresh assertion.
verifier_note: Quotes verified; engine.py l.155 is the _cmd_start check. Ch 30 l.29 already labels the reference's owner=True as 'Synthetic assertions', so it is evidence of the gap, not a separate defect. The R13-versus-schema conflict is real. Branch ADR-0007 defines Principal roles and ADR-0010 a reauth_max_age. Neither names the authenticator or signing-key custody, or protects the localhost API from same-user processes.

disposition.resolution: Partly resolved by ADR-0013: owner identity is a passphrase (scrypt hash outside the repo) with HttpOnly session cookie, CSRF token, login backoff and step-up for start, policy, capital, ownership and exception commands; R13 is resolved as 'authority = authenticated owner command in the hash-chained log'. The core socket maps tokens to roles (API token: OWNER; agent token: AGENT; strategy tokens bound to one artifact), and the core re-checks the step-up age for start and broker-admin actions. Login, session and CSRF are now tested over HTTP for the plugin routes, and the terminal's Playwright suite exercises login, HTTP 428 step-up and the same-id retry against a real API.
disposition.owner: I3 (owner authentication, ADR-0013) with I6 (agent OS isolation)
disposition.missing: The core trusts the authenticated_at_ns asserted by whoever holds the API token, and both token files are readable by any process of the same OS user, so a same-user agent can act as the owner (BR-OPS-04). Passkeys are deferred by ADR-0013.

title: Agent and research credential custody is unspecified: who holds model/data provider keys is never said, and the Mac setup gives workers no separate OS identity from the gateway

locations.quote: Research code runs without production secrets or network authority.
A source worker acquires licensed data.
the operating-system identity lacks broker credentials and order-service administrative access.
Store secrets in a suitable secret manager on AWS and the platform's protected credential storage on the Mac.
Restrict network egress for code experiments, mount datasets read-only where possible

explanation: Source and research workers must call OpenAI, xAI and data vendors, which needs network access and provider keys. CLAUDE.md's 'without ... network authority' fits generated experiment code (Ch 23 l.13) but not these workers, and the book never says which principal holds the provider keys. Those keys are spending authority. If workers hold them, an injected document can exfiltrate a key or spend outside any budget. Ch 19 l.15 requires the planner's OS identity to lack broker credentials. That needs separate OS users on the Mac, but the Mac layout (Ch 24 l.3-9) runs everything as the developer's user, alongside Claude Code. Same-user processes can read credentials kept in files, in environment variables, or in keychain items created through the security CLI.
proposed_resolution: Define three principals. (a) Execution gateway: a dedicated macOS user or launchd daemon with its own keychain; on AWS, its own instance role and Secrets Manager path. It is the only holder of broker credentials. (b) Model/data gateway: holds provider and vendor keys, enforces per-job allowances, and has egress only to allowlisted provider endpoints. (c) Research sandbox: a container or VM with no host keychain, no ledger socket and read-only datasets. Its only egress is the model/data gateway, and generated code inside it runs with no network. Workers receive short-lived, per-job_id capability tokens scoped to allowance and tools. Claude Code runs as a user that cannot read the gateway user's files and holds only paper credentials. Reword CLAUDE.md: 'Research code holds no broker, ledger or provider credentials and reaches the network only through the model/data gateway.' Set provider-side hard spend limits per key as a second layer. Negative tests: the sandbox cannot read the keychain or Secrets Manager, and direct egress to provider APIs is blocked.
verifier_note: Quotes verified. The original 'contradiction' depended on reading CLAUDE.md's 'research code' as all research workers; it can also mean generated experiment code, which agrees with Ch 23 l.13. Kind changed to omission. The keychain claim is narrowed: keychain items carry per-app ACLs. Severity lowered from critical to high because the Mac holds paper-only credentials (Ch 24 l.3) and paid calls are disabled by default.

disposition.resolution: Partly resolved by ADR-0016: agents hold no broker credentials and no ledger handle, may assert only AGENT on the core socket, and paid calls are disabled until the owner records a budget. Provider keys are read from an environment variable or a 0600 file under ~/.unknown/secrets, i.e. by the same OS user as the core.
disposition.missing: A separate OS identity or sandbox for agent workers and a model gateway that alone holds provider keys, with negative tests that a worker cannot read the core's token or the keys; provider-side hard spend limits recorded.

title: Stop and condition-block clearance is ambiguous: runbook 'latches' and the auth-expiry/restart flows auto-resume, while the green rules say only the owner clears a latch

locations.quote: Latch new-entry prohibition for the affected account, retain reservation
Resume only after a fresh reconciliation meets the approved tolerances.
The service must enter an authentication-required state, notify the owner and resume only after reconciliation.
It clears the latch only after the checks pass. An automatic process restart cannot clear it.
Starting after a stop requires owner authentication and a fresh state version.
A restart begins in reconciliation-required mode.
An automatically restarted process with unknown state is a recovery incident, not a successful deployment.

explanation: The book uses 'latch' and 'resume' loosely across five situations: the owner red stop, the unknown-order runbook, the mismatch runbook, IBKR daily re-authentication and supervisor restarts. One engineer would auto-resume after every daily IBKR restart or every resolved unknown order. Another would require owner green every time, which makes unattended operation impossible. The two give different money and authority outcomes. The book also does not say whether the account-scoped runbook latch is the same object as the global owner-cleared latch. Nor does it say whether a restart that finds a SUBMIT_PENDING outbox row may resume.
proposed_resolution: Use two durable mechanisms. (1) STOP latches, scoped global, account or session. They are set by owner red, loss or drawdown triggers, security incidents, restore, exception-accounting freezes, or an UNKNOWN order still unresolved after N minutes. Only an owner-authenticated green plus preflight clears them. (2) CONDITION blocks, scoped account, strategy or instrument, with a typed reason: AUTH_EXPIRED, PROCESS_RESTART, RECON_PENDING, DATA_STALE, MODEL_OUTAGE or UNKNOWN_ORDER. Each reason has a machine-checked clearing predicate. A block auto-clears only when its predicate passes, no latch is set in scope, and reconciliation shows no unexplained quantity or cash difference and no UNKNOWN order. A block whose resolution required a corrective economic event escalates to a latch. A scheduled IBKR restart raises AUTH_EXPIRED, which auto-clears after reconciliation. Weekly 2FA needs the owner but is not a latch. A crash restart that finds SUBMIT_PENDING or UNKNOWN escalates to a latch. Use a dedicated broker API username, so the owner's manual logins never evict the gateway. Test each reason.
verifier_note: Quotes verified. Branch ADR-0010 resolves part of this: a recovery gate, auto-resume defaulting to off, and a risk stop for reconciliation failure that sets the owner-only latch. It does not classify AUTH_EXPIRED or define the unknown-order runbook's account-scoped 'latch', so Ch 12 l.17 and Ch 26 l.19/l.23 remain open. That IBKR allows one session per username is an external fact; check it against S04/S06 before relying on it.

disposition.resolution: Same split as BR-ORD-17: the runbook defines a latch (cleared only by owner green with preflight) and a condition (cleared when the fact changes). A scheduled IBKR restart is a connectivity condition; a crash restart that finds SUBMIT_PENDING turns it UNKNOWN (blocking) and sets the owner recovery hold.
disposition.residual: An UNKNOWN order never escalates to a latch by itself; it blocks entries until broker evidence resolves it (BR-ORD-03).

title: Whether red triggers liquidation is ambiguous across chapters; who may set a latch is unspecified and paper_defaults.json has no emergency-policy field

locations.quote: A red stop latches a durable prohibition on new exposure and invokes a defined cancellation/reduction policy.
Stopping new entries and liquidating holdings are separate policies.
The configured emergency policy and its limitations are visible before activation.
Persist the aggregate stop, cancel entry orders and follow the approved reduction policy.
a compromised optional worker cannot clear the global stop latch.

explanation: Ch 0 l.19 says red invokes a 'cancellation/reduction policy'. Ch 22 l.28 says stopping and liquidating are separate policies. Ch 13 l.21 says 'A separate approved liquidation policy may submit risk-reducing orders' without saying whether red triggers it. Ch 22 requires the emergency policy to be shown before activation, but paper_defaults.json has no field for it. Ch 23 forbids workers only from clearing the latch, which implies they may set it. If setting the latch also triggers reduction, an injected agent can force liquidations, realizing losses and tax events. Without a clear rule, an engineer may wire red to market sells.
proposed_resolution: Default red blocks entries and cancels open entry orders, and sells nothing. Liquidation happens only through a separate owner command (red + reduce) or a signed-policy action tied to a deterministic risk trigger. Add to the policy and to paper_defaults.json: emergency_policy {owner_stop: CANCEL_ENTRIES, loss_trigger: CANCEL_ENTRIES|REDUCE_LIMIT, reduce: {only_reconciled_unreserved_long: true, collar_bps, max_child_qty, max_duration_s}}. The default is no automatic reduction. Principals that may set a latch: owner, risk supervisor, reconciliation service, security monitor. Agents and workers may only raise an alert, which the risk supervisor converts to a latch only by deterministic rule. The terminal shows the active emergency_policy next to the red control.
verifier_note: Quotes verified. Ch 0 versus Ch 22 is not a strict contradiction, because a 'cancellation/reduction policy' can be cancel-only. Kind changed to ambiguity. config/paper_defaults.json has no emergency or liquidation field. Branch ADR-0010 sets on_stop_liquidation default NONE. ADR-0007 limits red to OWNER and SYSTEM, and denies AGENT stop/start. The book text and paper defaults still need to match those decisions.

disposition.resolution: Red never liquidates: on_stop_liquidation must be NONE (other values are refused), working sells stay working and wind-down creates no new sell under a latch. Only OWNER and SYSTEM may issue stop; AGENT and STRATEGY are refused, and SYSTEM latches only from deterministic triggers in code.

title: No out-of-band stop path, no rule for a red received by a non-owning deployment, and no rule for broker-side cancels found on reconnect

locations.quote: The red control is always reachable and uses a short authenticated command path.
Do not expose broker management interfaces or the control API directly to the public internet.
On suspected credential compromise: latch the trading stop, revoke affected credentials through authorized channels

explanation: If the control host is hung or partitioned, or the owner is off the private network, a stop is needed most and the book gives no path to issue one. It has no runbook for stopping at the broker itself: broker cancel-all, disabling API access, or rotating the password. With two deployments, a red pressed in a terminal attached to the non-owning deployment latches a ledger that does not own the account, and still appears to succeed. On reconnect, the book does not say how to treat broker-side cancellations or position changes the system did not command. Ch 9 l.49 covers unknown external trades, not external cancels.
proposed_resolution: 1) The terminal always shows the owning deployment and epoch, and routes red to it. Test: partition the control host, cancel at the broker, reconnect, and assert the latch is set.
verifier_note: Quotes verified. 'Always reachable' in Ch 22 l.24 is plausibly a UI statement, so the claimed conflict with Ch 24 l.13 is dropped. The confirmed defects are omissions. Under ADR-0011 each deployment has its own database, so a red sent to the wrong deployment lands in the wrong ledger.

disposition.resolution: Partly resolved: RB-01 documents the out-of-band path (the broker's own interface: cancel all orders for the account), and after restart the core reconciles first; a cancel made at the broker arrives as a broker-confirmed CANCELED and releases the hold.
disposition.owner: I3 (terminal shows the owning deployment and routes red) with the OPS track (private remote access)
disposition.missing: A red pressed on a non-owning deployment latches only that deployment's database and reports success; no private phone-usable access path; unexplained broker-side cancels are accepted without latching.

title: Agent budget authority is open: model escalation, child-job allowances, pre-call reservation and exhaustion semantics are undefined

locations.quote: Workers cannot recursively create unbounded workers.
Escalate only when uncertainty or expected value justifies cost.
An agent may say that evidence supports increasing a budget or changing a parameter, with uncertainty and downside scenarios.
Infrastructure spending remains disabled until the owner supplies a budget.

explanation: Jobs carry a 'token/cost allowance', but the book does not say who sets it. It does not say whether a worker may spawn bounded child jobs with fresh allowances; the wording implies bounded recursion is allowed. It does not say who decides escalation to a model priced 5x higher (astra versus sol, on both input and output). If the worker decides, that is a budget self-increase. It does not say whether cost is reserved before a call or counted afterwards, or what exhaustion does. An engineer enforcing cloud_monthly_budget_cents by stopping instances could terminate the execution gateway while it has open orders.
proposed_resolution: Budgets are owner-signed policy. A deterministic scheduler assigns each job's allowance from a per-class quota, and workers cannot set or change it. Child jobs debit the parent's remaining allowance, with depth at most 1. Model escalation follows a router table (job class -> ordered model list with a per-class cost cap) and is never a worker decision. Before each call, the model gateway atomically reserves the worst-case cost (input x p_in + max_output_tokens including reasoning x p_out) against the daily and monthly caps. It releases the reservation against provider-reported usage. A timeout keeps the worst-case reservation, mirroring the order rule. Exhaustion rejects new paid jobs only and never touches execution, reconciliation or risk. Cloud-budget enforcement may stop research workers but only alerts for the execution host. Agents may emit only a BudgetRecommendation object. Tests: an allowance increase is rejected; a spawn chain is capped; a timeout keeps the reservation.
verifier_note: Quotes verified. The price ratio is 5x on both input and output ($10/$2 and $50/$10). Ch 27 schedules cost-capped cloud jobs for days 13-14, so this is in scope rather than a later track. It does not block the ledger and order foundation, and paid calls default to disabled (budget 0), so severity is lowered from high to medium. ADR-0007 bars AGENT from raising budgets but does not cover router escalation, child allowances or pre-call reservation.

disposition.resolution: ADR-0016: budgets are owner policy. Each call atomically reserves its worst-case cost against lifetime, monthly, daily, per-role, per-provider and per-job caps before the network call, and an unconfirmed call stays consumed until reconciled. A job's envelope cap can only lower the owner's per-job cap; child jobs have depth at most 1 and cannot widen the parent; routing uses owner-approved pinned ids only, never a worker decision. Agents cannot import execution or ledger code, so exhaustion never touches trading.

title: Budget fields disagree on period, type and scale, and integer cents cannot account per-call model costs

locations.quote: "paid_model_daily_budget_cents": 0,
The owner must still supply actual broker entities/account types, live authorized capital, monthly data/model/cloud budgets
"paid_service_budgets_approved": false,
`authorized_capital`, `operating_budget`, `policy_version`

explanation: The model budget appears in four forms: daily in the config, monthly in Ch 29, a boolean approval in the deployment record, and a single 'operating_budget' in Ch 1. The sol job costs $0.004 + $0.002 = $0.006 (0.6 cents). Booking each call in integer cents either floors it to 0, so spend goes unrecorded and a positive budget never binds, or rounds it up, overcounting a luna call about 33x.

title: The promotion transition authority matrix is undefined: the author can be its own evaluator, and production learning can change parameters without a new hashed artifact

locations.quote: Transitions require evidence references and an authority identity.
The evaluator has read access to results and write access to evidence, while the promotion service enforces a separate immutable policy.
Production learning is limited to approved estimators and bounded parameter rules; generated code remains review-only.
Every candidate has a unique hash over executable artifact or approved configuration, dependency lock, feature definitions and strategy schema.

explanation: The book lists eight statuses but not which principal may perform each transition. Ch 20 l.29 forbids changing the pass threshold. Nothing requires the evaluator principal to differ from the author, so the research worker that wrote a candidate could also evaluate it and write its own evidence. Nothing stops the critic being the same model family as the author, which correlates approval. Ch 19's 'bounded parameter rules' for production learning do not say each parameter update becomes a new hashed artifact, so live parameters can drift with nothing to audit against the Ch 20 identity rule.
proposed_resolution: Transition matrix. proposed->reproducible->validated: evaluator principal only; it must differ from the author principal and runs a pinned manifest it cannot edit. validated->paper: the promotion service if the class is inside the owner envelope, otherwise an owner signature. paper->eligible: an owner signature for the first artifact in a class, then the promotion service within the same envelope. eligible->active: promotion service. any->quarantined: any service. quarantined->eligible: owner only. Evidence is append-only, keyed by (candidate_hash, manifest_hash), and only the evaluator principal may write it. The critic uses a different provider family when one is available. Each online parameter update is a new parameter artifact with its own hash. The promotion service checks it against the approved domain before use and journals it.
verifier_note: Quotes verified. The claim that bounded learning contradicts hash identity is overstated, because Ch 20 l.27 allows choosing a validated parameter artifact inside a domain. The defect is that production learning never says it produces such artifacts. Promotion is outside the first foundation; severity lowered to medium.

disposition.resolution: Resolved. The promotion transition table (RULES) fixes who may move an artifact and with which evidence: up to validated only the SYSTEM evaluator or the OWNER, and never the artifact's author; paper, eligible and active need a fresh owner approval; agents may propose and file evidence but never approve or transition, and agent-filed evidence never satisfies a gate. Evidence and transitions are append-only (database triggers) and keyed by artifact and protocol hash; any parameter change is a new spec hash and so a new artifact.
disposition.residual: Evaluator and author are distinguished by principal id; separate evaluator credentials are not built. No online learning exists, so no online parameter update path exists to guard.

title: Nothing stops the coding agent from merging or deploying production code, and release-signing key custody is unspecified

locations.quote: Research-generated code runs in an isolated environment. It may produce a candidate artifact and tests, but cannot merge itself or deploy to production.
Build reproducibly where practical and sign release artifacts.
On an unknown production binary: stop activation and compare signed artifact identity with the approved registry.
